Abstract 14

Purpose: To evaluate the association between surgically acquired neurological deficits and 15

mortality among patients who underwent surgical resection of brain metastases. 16

17

Methods: Patients who underwent surgical resection of brain metastases at our institution 18

between 2011 and 2019 were included. Surgically acquired neurological deficits were defined 19

as dysarthria/aphasia, ataxia, hemiparesis, and visual field loss. A Cox proportional hazards 20

model adjusting for potential confounders was constructed to evaluate whether surgically 21

acquired neurological deficits were independently associated with a higher risk of overall 22

mortality. 23

24

Results: A total of 153 patients were included in the analysis. 3.3% (5 patients) had a 25

surgically acquired neurological deficit. On univariate time-to-event analysis, there was no 26

statistically significant association between the development of a surgically acquired 27

neurological deficit and mortality (HR=1.12; 95% CI=0.15, 8.24; p=0.910). On multivariate 28

time-to-event analysis adjusting for potential confounders, there was also no statistically 29

significant association between the development of a surgically acquired neurological deficit 30

and mortality (HR=1.53; 95% CI=0.20, 11.9; p=0.683). 31

32

Conclusion: The development of a surgically acquired neurological deficit was not 33

associated with overall mortality. Although this conclusion differs from other studies in the 34

literature, the goal of surgical resection remains unchanged – to resect as much tumor as 35

possible while still preserving neurological function. 36

37

Keywords: brain cancer, brain tumor, quality of life, function, activities of daily living 38

Introduction 39

Brain metastases are the most common type of brain malignancies in adults,1 occurring in 20% 40

to 40% of cancer patients throughout the course of their disease.2 Among adults, the 41

commonest sites of origin of cerebral metastases are the lung and breast.3 Surgical resection 42

is central to the management of brain metastasis as it confers survival benefit,4-7 allows for 43

the relief of symptoms,8 and allows for the establishment of a definitive diagnosis.8 However, 44

there is also a significant risk of a surgically acquired neurological deficit. 45

The incidence of a surgically acquired neurological deficit has been reported to be 46

approximately 6%.9,10 Preservation of neurological function is important due to its potential 47

implications on function and quality of life.11 Surgically acquired neurological deficits have 48

also recently been shown to increase the risk of mortality.12 Medikonda et al. reported a 49

statistically significant association between surgically acquired neurological deficits and 50

overall mortality among patients who underwent surgical resection of a solitary brain 51

metastasis.12 However, while the findings of Medikonda et al. are significant in that they 52

were the first to show that surgically acquired neurological deficits increase the risk of 53

mortality among patients with solitary brain metastases, their findings have thus far not been 54

validated. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the association between surgically acquired 55

neurological deficits and mortality among patients who underwent surgical resection of brain 56

metastases. 57

58

Methods 59

Study design 60

This was a retrospective study of patients who underwent surgical resection of brain 61

metastases at our institution between March 2011 and December 2019. Institutional ethics 62

approval was obtained from the local institutional review board prior to the commencement 63

2020/00358), and a waiver of informed consent was granted as this study posed no more than 65

minimal risk to participants. 66

67

Cohort selection 68

The operating theatre records database was accessed to retrieve the National Registration 69

Identity Card numbers (NRICs, which act as the national identification number), date of 70

surgery, provisional diagnosis, operation summaries, and surgical codes of all patients who 71

underwent surgery for a brain tumor. The medical records of the patients were then retrieved 72

and screened for inclusion in the study. The inclusion criteria were (a) patients who had a 73

histologically verified metastasis to the brain, and (b) patients who were 18 years old and 74

above at the time of surgery. The exclusion criteria were (a) patients who presented only with 75

leptomeningeal or skull metastases, and (b) patients who were followed up for less than 28 76

days. 77

78

Data collection 79

Clinical data were collected using a standardized data collection form. Variables collected 80

include (1) demographics (including age at the time of surgical resection, sex, and ethnicity), 81

(2) details of the extent of disease (including the presence of systemic disease at the time of 82

surgery and the size of the largest brain metastasis), (3) duration of hospitalization, (4) site of 83

the primary tumor (defined as the 5 commonest sites and ‘others’), (5) and presence of 84

preoperative and postoperative neurological deficits, and (6) whether the patient passed away. 85

Preoperative and postoperative neurological deficits were defined as dysarthria/aphasia, 86

ataxia, hemiparesis, or visual field loss.12 A surgically acquired neurological deficit was 87

defined as a neurological deficit that developed only after surgical resection. 88

Statistical analysis 90

The baseline characteristics of the patients were reported using mean and standard deviation 91

for continuous variables and count numbers and percentages for categorical variables. 92

Hypothesis testing was conducted using the Fisher’s exact test. A p-value of 0.05 or less was 93

taken to be statistically significant. 94

To ascertain whether the presence of a surgically acquired neurological deficit was 95

associated with overall mortality, Cox regression models were constructed, adjusting for age 96

and variables that had a statistically significant association with presence of surgically 97

acquired neurological deficits on univariate analysis. A p-value of 0.05 or less was taken to 98

be statistically significant. For patients who demised during the follow-up period, time-to- 99

mortality was defined as the duration between the first surgical resection and the date of 100

death as documented in the electronic medical records. For patients who did not demise 101

during the follow-up period, time-to-mortality was defined as the duration between the date 102

of the first surgical resection of and the date of the latest follow-up. All data analyses were 103

conducted using R Studio Version 1.2.5042. 104

105

Results 106

Baseline characteristics of the study population 107

The baseline characteristics of patients with and without surgically acquired neurological 108

deficit(s) were reported in Table 1. A total of 153 patients met the inclusion criteria for this 109

study. The mean (SD) age was 59.5 (11.7) years, and 81 (52.9%) patients were female. The 110

incidence of a surgically acquired neurological deficit was 3.3% (5 patients). Details on the 111

clinical course of the 5 patients with a surgically acquired neurological deficit were presented 112

in Table 2. 113

Association between surgically acquired neurological deficit and 115

On univariate time-to-event analysis, there was no statistically significant association 116

between the development of a surgically acquired neurological deficit and mortality 117

(HR=1.12; 95% CI=0.15, 8.24; p=0.910) (Table 3). On multivariate time-to-event analysis 118

adjusting for potential confounders, there was also no statistically significant association 119

between the development of a surgically acquired neurological deficit and mortality 120

(HR=1.53; 95% CI=0.20, 11.9; p=0.683) (Table 3). 121

On subgroup analysis of patients who presented with solitary brain metastasis (86 122

patients, 56.2%), there was no statistically significant association between surgically acquired 123

neurological deficit and overall mortality on both univariate (HR=1.12; 95% CI=0.15, 8.26; 124

p=0.909) and multivariate analysis (HR=1.51; 95% CI=0.19, 11.8; p=0.695). 125

126

Discussion 127

In this study of patients who underwent surgical resection of brain metastases, we showed 128

that there was no statistically significant association between the development of a surgically 129

acquired neurological deficit and overall mortality. Our findings differ from the findings of 130

Medikonda et al.12 In their study of patients who underwent surgical resection of a solitary 131

brain metastasis, Medikonda et al.12 reported that a surgically acquired neurological deficit 132

was significantly associated with a higher risk of overall mortality. In our study, we followed 133

Medikonda et al.’s definition of neurological deficit,12 except that we considered dysarthria a 134

neurological deficit as well. 135

The association between a surgically acquired neurological deficit and mortality has 136

been postulated to be due to the confounding effect of the quality of life.13 Patients with 137

surgically acquired neurological deficits have a higher risk of mortality because these patients 138

also tend to have poorer quality of life, and a poorer quality of life has been associated with a 139

higher risk of mortality.13 However, the retrospective nature of Medikonda et al.’s12 and our 140

study make the assessment of the quality of life difficult, and therefore it is unclear whether 141

the association between surgically acquired neurological deficits may be attributed to the 142

confounding effect of quality of life. Prospective studies that assess and control for the 143

quality of life in the analysis may help clarify this association. 144

However, one should be cognizant of the goal of surgical treatment when interpreting 145

studies on the effect of surgically acquired neurological deficits on mortality. As Liau pointed 146

out, whether surgically acquired neurological deficits actually impact survival is practically 147

irrelevant, as the goal of surgical resection has been and should continue to be to resect as 148

much tumor as possible while still maintaining neurological function, regardless of whether 149

or not the length of overall survival is significantly impacted by the acquisition of a new 150

neurological deficit.14 151

There are several limitations to our study. First, the small sample size of our cohort 152

limited the statistical power of our analyses, with only 5 patients having a surgically acquired 153

neurological deficit. Also, as our study included only patients from a single institution, the 154

results may not be generalizable to other institutions. Lastly, we do not rule out the possibility 155

of undocumented surgically acquired neurological deficits, and therefore the incidence of 156

surgically acquired neurological deficits may be lower than the actual incidence reported in 157

this study. 158

159

Conclusions 160

The development of a surgically acquired neurological deficit was not associated with overall 161

mortality. Although this conclusion differs from other studies in the literature, the goal of 162
